name: Filesystem allowlist
claim_class: A claim that a build agent's filesystem access stayed within its intended scope.
proof_obligation: The enforcing form is permissions configuration plus a PreToolUse hook. Neither is built yet, so today this rule is carried by the prompt, which is the weakest form of it and the form this catalog argues against. The record says prompt because that is what is true. An agent never reads, writes, lists, traverses, moves, copies, or deletes anything inside a synced or personal folder, or anywhere outside an explicit allowlist, no matter what it is looking for. The allowlist categories, adapted per project: the git repository and the parent folder holding directories the build reads and writes; the language toolchain and package caches, readable and executable, writing only to their own cache locations; standard system paths for the tools the build runs; the session's scratch directory and the agent's own state directory; and outbound network access limited to the package registries the build needs. Everything else is off limits. If a specification or reference file appears to live somewhere off the allowlist, the agent reports that it is not available in the repository and asks, instead of reaching outside the allowlist to go find it.
failure_mode: A synced or personal folder replicates every change it receives to every other device and into its own history, so a wrong write, or even a well-intentioned reorganization, corrupts the canonical copies of those documents everywhere at once, not in just one place. The risk is not only that work strays outside its intended scope; it is quiet corruption of documents that are the source of truth for something entirely outside the project. A build agent has no reason to be in a folder like that at all, so treating it as somewhere the agent might read from also leaves it somewhere the agent could write to.
origin_incident: A delivery report stated that specification files could not be found in a synced personal folder, which meant the agent had gone looking for them there. Treating a location as somewhere to read from means it could just as easily become somewhere to write to.
